articles.title: Europe has 11 ways to choke Russia’s war. It doesn’t need Trump’s permission for any of them - Euromaidan Press
articles.summary: Europe has 11 ways to choke Russia’s war. It doesn’t need Trump’s permission for any of them  Euromaidan Press
articles.full_text:
On 9 October, three weeks after signing the first major Russia oil sanctions in two years, Donald Trump agreed with Vladimir Putin to bring Russian diesel back to world markets. The US Treasury suspended its sanctions on that trade until April 2027 the same day. In the two days before, Russian strikes had killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians.
Europe answered on 12 October with its largest sanctions package yet: nearly 1,600 new listings, almost all in Russia’s military-industrial complex. Its core, says Ukraine’s sanctions envoy Vladyslav Vlasiuk, is Russia’s missile program and the electronics inside it, from capacitors to semiconductors. Six in ten listings came from Ukrainian proposals, and Brussels adopted them within weeks.
That is the right reflex, and proof that Europe can move fast when it chooses. But the package names companies and people one by one. On the measures that cut whole sectors, the ones that would hurt Moscow most, Europe still waits for Washington.
It waits for Trump to decide whether to enforce the Graham Act he signed in September. It waits for him to decide whether to lean on Hungary and Slovakia or let them off. It waits for the G7 to rule on tanker services before touching its own ships. Europe keeps asking the Trump administration to decide things it is perfectly able to decide itself.
If the EU is serious about ending a war on its own continent, it does not need a miracle from Washington. It needs to pull the levers already in its hands. Here they are.
1. Fix export-control enforcement on dual-use goods. It is unacceptable that the newest Russian drones and missiles contain not only Chinese parts but American and European ones. The "War and Sanctions" portal logs what turns up. The EU should find and close the enforcement gaps in its own dual-use export law. Choking the supply to Russia's war industry serves Ukraine and Europe alike.
2. Force Hungary and Slovakia off Russian oil. The EU banned Russian oil imports in 2022, with temporary exemptions for landlocked states: Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary. Czechia has since diversified and dropped Russian oil entirely. Slovakia and Hungary can do the same; the Czech case proves it is a question of will, not feasibility. Ending the exemptions would also make good on REPowerEU's central promise, phasing out Russian energy. The gas-import ban is already decided. Oil is the gap that remains.
3. Close the Greek and Maltese tanker loophole. Up to 40% of Russia's seaborne oil travels on European tankers, Greek and Maltese. The EU has banned maritime services for Russian oil since 2022, with one exception: cargoes sold below the price cap. This spring the Council discussed scrapping that exception, which would have meant a full ban, then made any change conditional on coordination with the G7. Once again, Europe is asking Washington to act for it. The EU should overcome Greek and Maltese resistance and ban every maritime service for Russian oil: transport, insurance, and the rest.
4. Stop the shadow fleet in European waters. Russia ships oil to India, China, and Türkiye through a shadow fleet of aging, often uninsured tankers. Europe can check their insurance and turn away any that lack EU or G7 cover, especially in the North Sea and the Baltic, where any spill would be an ecological disaster, and an uninsured operator would not pay for it.
Patrols in territorial waters and exclusive economic zones have to be reinforced. Russia also uses these ships for espionage, sabotage, and damage to undersea infrastructure. Strengthen NATO's Baltic Sentry. Consider adding a maritime operation by the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force or the Coalition of the Willing across the North and Baltic Seas and the Skagerrak, before the Danish straits. If the Russian Baltic Fleet escalates, Europe should be ready for confrontation. Moscow should hear that it is not feared and that it will be stopped. At sea, it is weaker than even NATO's Baltic Sea states alone, never mind NATO's European members together.
5. Scrap the Lingen nuclear-fuel deal. In July, Lower Saxony approved a plan for the French state company Framatome to make nuclear fuel jointly with Rosatom, Russia's builder of nuclear weapons, at Lingen. It is dressed up as serving REPowerEU, since the venture lets Hungary, Slovakia, and Bulgaria buy fuel from a Franco-Russian joint operation instead of straight from Rosatom.
This is nonsense. Ukraine was once wholly dependent on Russian nuclear fuel and diversified fast; Finland and Czechia have done the same. Hungary, Slovakia, and Bulgaria can follow. Stretching the dependence out and hiding it behind a French partner is the opposite of what REPowerEU is for. Lower Saxony's own environment minister called the deal "grundfalsch," fundamentally wrong.
6. Build a Ukraine Fund from frozen Russian assets. Supporting Ukraine will cost more next year, not less, so it is time to get serious about Russia's frozen assets. Not confiscation, which European capitals still resist, and not a simple transfer to Kyiv, which amounts to the same thing, but a dedicated EU-run Ukraine Fund that could invest these assets and use them better than they are used now. ICUV has set it all out in a policy paper.
7. Adopt the Graham-bill sanctions. Sanction every Russian state company (majority or controlling state stake) and every Russian oligarch who has not taken a public anti-war stand. Forbes counts 155 Russian billionaires.
8. Cut every Russian and Belarusian bank off SWIFT. Russia still has 301 operating banks, yet only 103 Russian banks and financial institutions sit under the EU's transaction ban, and just a handful of Belarusian ones. Gazprombank, which the US Treasury says pays Russia's soldiers, is still not on the EU list. Stop listing banks one by one: disconnect the entire Russian and Belarusian banking systems and put them under a full transaction ban, with narrow exceptions for food, medicine, and humanitarian trade.
9. End land transit to and from Russia, Kaliningrad included. Stop all overland freight, rail and road, between the EU and Russia. Baltic ports should carry no Russian trade at all, not just grain. Halt the gas transit to Kaliningrad through Lithuania's pipelines, too; let it arrive by sea, where Russia already runs an LNG terminal. Winters are mild now, so the real effect is mostly higher costs, and even that is worth doing.
10. Ban visas for Russian (ex-)servicemen and their families. The EU's 21st sanctions package laid the legal basis in July and then set no start date. Bring it into force, and extend it to the families.
11. Launch the Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression and the Claims Commission. Speed up the creation of, and accession to, the tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine, and the convention establishing a Claims Commission.
Europe cannot escape this burden. A Russian victory, even a partial one such as a peace on Moscow's terms, would cost it far more than helping Ukraine to a partial victory of its own, a peace along the line of contact. If Europe wants the war to end, it has to lead, alongside Ukraine, instead of waiting on a miracle from the Trump administration. The tools are already in its hands.

Kyiv, Ukraine - A 13-year-old girl was among three people killed in a Russian strike on a house near the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine on Monday, the authorities said, as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned of Russia's next pressure-related move.
A 13-year-old girl was among three people killed in a Russian strike on a house near the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine on Monday, the authorities said.
The head of the Donetsk regional military administration, Vadym Filashkin, said a house in the Cherkaske area was hit with cluster munitions, accusing Russia of "a deliberate attempt" to maximize civilian casualties.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Monday that Russia would only negotiate "seriously" under pressure, days after President Donald Trump announced a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel.
"For Germany and for Europe, such a decision is out of the question," said Merz, referring to the US-Russia diesel deal.

Trump then on Sunday claimed Russia and Ukraine agreed to an "energy ceasefire," to which Zelensky said was "news for me." Quickly after the announcement, Ukraine claimed Russia attacked again "after" the alleged ceasefire.
Asked whether he now regarded Trump as being on Russia's side, rather than a mediator in the Ukraine war, Merz merely noted the conflict was not yet over.
"It has not ended in the way President Trump intended it to within just a few days at the start of his second term," he said.

articles.title: How Has the Ukraine War Changed Russia-India Relations? - Russia Post
articles.summary: How Has the Ukraine War Changed Russia-India Relations?  Russia Post
articles.full_text:
The Kremlin’s war against Ukraine has transformed Russia’s historical relationship with India. While discounted Russian oil has driven trade to record highs, defense ties have weakened.
In September, Vladimir Putin traveled to New Delhi, where he met Indian PM Narendra Modi on the sidelines of a BRICS summit. It was the leaders’ second meeting in less than two weeks: on August 31, they had held talks during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek. In New Delhi, they visited INNOPROM India, a Russian industrial exhibition being held in India for the first time. Putin and Modi discussed trade, energy, defense and industrial cooperation and reiterated their intention to increase bilateral trade to $100 billion by 2030.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, trade between Russia and India stood at around $10 billion a year. By the 2024-25 fiscal year, it had surged to $69 billion. Yet almost all of the growth was attributable to Russian oil, which had played only a minor role in relations before the war.
The Soviet legacy
The present-day relationship has its roots in the Cold War. After gaining independence from Britain in 1947, India declined to join either of the two opposing blocs. New Delhi sought to maintain relations with both superpowers while determining its own positions on questions of international affairs. In 1961, India became a founding member of the Nonaligned Movement.
India was never a Soviet ally in the sense that the Warsaw Pact countries were. Nevertheless, relations between New Delhi and Moscow gradually grew closer over the decades. The USSR helped India build steel and aluminum plants, power transmission lines and hydroelectric stations, while also supporting the development of Indian heavy industry and supplying weapons to the Indian army. These contacts took place against the backdrop of US cooperation with Pakistan. Washington concluded military agreements with Islamabad and supplied it with weapons. During the 1971 war between India and Pakistan over East Pakistan (now Bangladesh), Moscow backed New Delhi, while Richard Nixon’s administration effectively leaned toward Pakistan.
The USSR also mediated after the previous India-Pakistan conflict over Kashmir in 1965, organizing the 1966 Tashkent summit that culminated in a peace settlement known as the Tashkent Declaration. In addition, Moscow repeatedly used its veto on the UN Security Council between 1957 and 1971 to support India’s position, primarily in relation to Kashmir.
The ideological component of the relationship disappeared after the Soviet Union collapsed, but military cooperation survived. Russia continued supplying India with fighter aircraft, tanks, submarines, missiles and air defense systems. It also transferred some technology and arranged for Russian equipment to be produced under license in India. A symbol of Russia-India military ties, the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile, emerged from a joint project started in the 1990s. From the standpoint of India, Russia had a leg up on Western countries, as it could offer weapons cheaper, placed fewer restrictions on their use and was willing to transfer certain sensitive technologies.
Changing arms supply landscape
From the Soviet collapse through the 2000s, Russia remained India’s principal arms supplier, accounting for around three quarters of its imports of major weapons. But New Delhi gradually began diversifying its suppliers to lessen that dependence. Other considerations included gaining access to more advanced systems and developing the local defense industry. Russia faced growing competition from France, Israel and the US.
Even in 2016-20, Moscow provided 51% of India’s imports of major weapons. In 2021-25, that figure had fallen to 40%, however. At the same time, India remains Russia’s largest customer, accounting for 48% of all Russian exports of major weapons in 2021-25.
The Ukraine war gave New Delhi more reasons to diversify away from Russia. Western sanctions imposed after the Russian invasion complicated payments to Russia: Indian banks and firms found it harder to conduct transactions in dollars, while switching to rupees and rubles failed to resolve the problem completely. In April 2023, for instance, it emerged that more than $2 billion in Indian payments had been held up for about a year because Moscow and New Delhi could not find a settlement mechanism acceptable to both sides and free of sanctions risks. In addition, Russia’s defense sector has become increasingly focused on supplying its own armed forces and encumbered by restrictions on imports of components for weapons and their production, ranging from microchips and optics to machine tools and engines.
Take the example of ordered S-400 air defense systems: in 2023, the Indian air force told a parliamentary committee that Moscow had informed it in writing that a “major delivery” could not be completed on schedule because of the war in Ukraine. Though the committee’s report did not identify the equipment, Indian media subsequently reported that it was referring to S-400 systems. India had ordered five of them for approximately $5.4 billion and originally expected to receive the whole order by end 2024. The fourth arrived only in June 2026, while the fifth and final system is expected in November 2026.
Still, much of the Indian military’s equipment is of Soviet or Russian origin. This was on display in the 2025 confrontation with Pakistan after a terrorist attack in Kashmir, when the Indian armed forces used Soviet and Russian systems like the Su-30MKI and MiG-29 fighter aircraft, as well as the S-400 and older air defense systems. New Delhi continues to buy Russian weapons, even though it is simultaneously increasing purchases from France, Israel and the US and seeking to move arms production to India.
Modi and Putin in 2025
India's Prime Minister's Office
Russian energy exports to India
In 2021, Russia provided only around 2% of India’s crude oil imports. Geography worked against it: it was far easier for India to buy oil from nearby producers such as Iraq, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Everything changed after February 2022, however. European countries began phasing out Russian energy imports and introduced a price cap on Russian oil. Moscow had to redirect enormous export volumes from Europe to Asia at short notice and offered discounts to attract new buyers. Indian refineries seized the opportunity. Within two years, Russia’s share of Indian crude imports had risen to nearly 35% (as of the 2023-24 fiscal year).
During the first nine months of 2023, Russian oil cost Indian buyers an average of approximately $526 per metric ton, including shipping and insurance, versus around $564 for Iraqi oil. Just in that period, buying Russian rather than Iraqi crude could have saved Indian companies about $2.7 billion. In the fiscal year ending in March 2026, Russia still accounted for about a third of India’s crude imports. That share ballooned to roughly half in July as disruptions curtailed supplies from the Middle East.
Before the Ukraine war, bilateral trade stood at around $10 billion. By the 2024-25 fiscal year, it had reached approximately $69 billion (before slipping back to about $60 billion in the 2025-26 fiscal year). Most of the increase owes to Russian exports to India, particularly oil and other energy commodities. Meanwhile, Indian exports to Russia grew much more slowly, leading to an enormous trade imbalance.
Besides supplying the domestic market, Indian refiners turned Russian crude into diesel, jet fuel and other products bound for Europe. According to S&P Global, the value of Indian petroleum-product exports to Europe more than tripled from about $5.9 billion in 2019 to $20.5 billion in 2024. European rules permitted imports of petroleum products refined from Russian crude in a third country, but that ended this year.
What else Moscow has to offer India
Nuclear energy remains one of the biggest areas of Russia-India cooperation. Rosatom designed six reactors with a combined capacity of around 6 gigawatts for the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant in southern India and is supplying major equipment. The first two reactors are already operating, while the others are at various stages of construction. In addition, Moscow and New Delhi are discussing the construction of another Russian-designed nuclear power plant at a new site in India.
Another area of Russia-India cooperation is the development of transport routes that would make bilateral trade cheaper and less dependent on Europe. The principal project is the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), which would run to Russia from India via the Arabian Sea, the Gulf of Oman, Iran and the Caspian Sea. The INSTC could significantly reduce delivery times compared with the traditional route through the Suez Canal and around Europe. The project has been under discussion for more than two decades but remains far from completion amid infrastructure and customs issues, as well as sanctions risks. Nevertheless, the importance of the INSTC for Moscow has increased markedly since 2022, as Russia looks for trade routes that bypass Europe. Moscow and New Delhi are also discussing the so-called Eastern Maritime Corridor (EMC) between Vladivostok and Chennai. For Russia, it offers an opportunity to sell India more coal, liquefied natural gas, oil and other Far East resources. The two sides have also agreed to expand cooperation in the Russian Far East in mining, energy, agriculture, diamonds and shipping.
Moscow is trying to diversify the range of goods it supplies. Russia has already become a major exporter of fertilizers and coal to India, while the two countries are discussing joint production of urea, a key nitrogen fertilizer for Indian agriculture. articles.title: Russia resumes diesel fuel supplies to Uzbekistan in September - UzDaily.uz
articles.summary: Russia resumes diesel fuel supplies to Uzbekistan in September  UzDaily.uz
articles.full_text:
Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan resumed imports of Russian diesel fuel in September 2026 after a month-long pause, purchasing around 26,000 tonnes, according to data published by the Geostatistics Telegram channel.
Total Russian diesel fuel deliveries to Central Asian countries and Mongolia reached 427,000 tonnes in September, compared with 371,000 tonnes in August, an increase of approximately 15.1%.
Mongolia was the largest buyer, receiving around 220,000 tonnes, up from 215,000 tonnes a month earlier. Kazakhstan imported 77,000 tonnes, compared with 28,000 tonnes in August.
Deliveries to Kyrgyzstan amounted to 67,000 tonnes, down from 72,000 tonnes, while Tajikistan received 38,000 tonnes, compared with more than 56,000 tonnes a month earlier.
No Russian diesel fuel was delivered to Uzbekistan in August. In September, the country rejoined the list of recipients of the petroleum product within regional trade.
According to Reuters, the increase in exports is linked to an oversupply of diesel fuel on the Russian market and falling prices.
However, the published data do not specify the value of supplies to Uzbekistan, the importing companies or the terms of the contracts signed.
The reported total volume of Russian diesel fuel deliveries to Central Asian countries reached 3 million tonnes in January–September 2026.
The September total cited above includes Mongolia, which is geographically outside Central Asia.
Across the four countries in the region—Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan—combined imports of Russian diesel fuel amounted to approximately 208,000 tonnes.

articles.title: Armenia’s Pashinyan: Severing our relations with Russia was not, is not, will not be among objectives - NEWS.am
articles.summary: Armenia’s Pashinyan: Severing our relations with Russia was not, is not, will not be among objectives  NEWS.am

It is unrealistic to hold a referendum at this time. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said this in an interview with Radio France Internationale (RFI), referring to the claims of Russian officials regarding a need for Armenia holding a referendum on relations with the European Union (EU).
“If you ask me a question, say: ‘Is the Republic of Armenia ready to be a member of the European Union today?’ I will honestly say that no, because we still need to implement many reforms in order to meet those standards; that is, applying in itself already implies a certain level of maturity of the process. Simply applying for the sake of applying is not very logical, especially since we are very actively working with the EU to implement reforms in our country as effectively as possible,” Pashinyan noted.
Also, he said that the objectives were not, are not, and will not be to break or worsen Armenia’s relations with Russia.
"On the contrary, we want to develop our relations with Russia. We simply need to record: regardless of everything, regardless of political leadership, our relations with Russia cannot be the same as before. What has changed is that there was a conflict with Azerbaijan before, now there is peace," said Nikol Pashinyan.
As for the statements coming from Russia that "Armenia can become a second Ukraine," the Armenian premier noted: "I believe and am convinced that such a thing will not happen."

articles.title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’ - The Guardian
articles.summary: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.
In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.
Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.
Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.
The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.
The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.
The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe, reported on Sunday that the US is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.
On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.
Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.
The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.
He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”
Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”
Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.
Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.
Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.
Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.
Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.
- Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

Russia wants to ruin the existing security architecture in Europe to make sure that Russian domination comes back to where it was before 1989. We have no doubt about it….
This is the moment when the entire west, Europe, the United States must show Russia’s Putin that we are ready for a deterrence policy with even harder measures – and I mean mainly sanctions.

Zelensky cited a drone strike on power plant in Kyiv, causing power outages, and an assault on a power plant in the second city of Kharkiv.
Attacks continued on Monday morning. Residents in several streets in Izyum, south-east of Kharkiv, lost power. At least 12 people were injured in Kharkiv city.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region in southeast Ukraine, Russia attacked three districts more than 10 times with artillery and drones, causing fires. In the north of the Zhytomyr region, Russian forces have been repeatedly shelling since Sunday evening, including attacks on railway and energy infrastructure.
UPDATE 0526 GMT:
Russia suffered a loss of more than 50,000 military personnel in September, including more than 28,000 soldiers killed, reports a NATO official.
The total is the highest in 2026. Ukraine’s General Staff estimated 46,230 Russian personnel losses during the month. The General Staff did not give a number of fatalities.
The NATO official said Ukraine’s armed forces suffered 5,000 casualties last month.
UPDATE 0520 GMT:
The toll has risen to three civilians killed, including two teenagers, and 25 injured from a Russian missile strike near Ukraine’s second city Kharkiv on Sunday.
The slain were a 16-year-old boy and two women aged 19 and 51. The missile landed near a grocery store and several residential buildings.
Among the injured were two girls aged 13 and 9.

Trump posted on social media on Sunday, “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed.”
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky pushed back the claim:
The ceasefire announcement was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire Ukraine will agree. If President Trump negotiated it with Putin — please tell us when the ceasefire begins — we are ready and we will accept it.
A senior Ukrainian official said, “Just now our repair teams are restoring electricity and water supplies in Kyiv [following Russian strikes].” He emphasized that “nobody has heard” of the ceasefire.

Russia is stalling on the battlefield and striking civilians far behind the front lines.

Senior Ukrainian officials met Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami, Florida on Friday and Saturday to discuss the proposal. articles.title: Tashkent to host second China–Central Asia trade expo - UzDaily.uz
articles.summary: Tashkent to host second China–Central Asia trade expo  UzDaily.uz
articles.full_text:
Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — The second China–Central Asia (Uzbekistan) 2026 Trade Exhibition will be held at the Tashkent International Exhibition Centre from 14 to 16 October.
Around 200 Chinese companies from 19 provinces, autonomous regions and centrally administered municipalities of China will participate, the organisers said at a press conference.
The exhibition is organised by the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT). The first edition was held in 2025, making this the second consecutive year Uzbekistan has hosted the event.
The organisers intend the exhibition to serve as a specialised platform for strengthening trade and economic cooperation, developing business contacts between China and Central Asian countries, and promoting industrial cooperation.
Exhibition marks anniversary of China–Uzbekistan partnership
Liu Yue, chief representative of the CCPIT representative office in Kazakhstan, said the event was being organised in accordance with agreements reached by the leaders of China and Uzbekistan.
It is intended to put into practice the outcomes of the China–Central Asia Summit and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, deepen China’s trade and economic ties with Uzbekistan and other countries in the region, and advance the development of a closer China–Central Asia community with a shared future.
Liu Yue said holding the exhibition for a second consecutive year reflected China’s determination to expand its presence in the Central Asian market and make bilateral cooperation more substantive and far-reaching.
She also thanked Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, which is supporting the event, as well as the Tashkent Region Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the Economic Committee and the industrial association for helping prepare the exhibition and facilitate cooperation between companies from the two countries.
The exhibition is taking place in the year marking the 10th anniversary of comprehensive strategic partnership relations between China and Uzbekistan. In addition, 2026 has been designated as a year for high-quality development of cooperation between China and Central Asian countries.
According to the organisers, at the SCO Council of Heads of State meeting on 31 August, the leaders of the two countries outlined a course towards a new “golden decade” of bilateral relations. The press release said both countries, guided by the “China–Central Asia spirit”, were expanding opportunities for cooperation in trade liberalisation, industrial investment and green development.
Bilateral trade triples in seven years as China remains Uzbekistan’s largest investor
Azamat Rakhmonov, head of the department for cooperation with China at Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, outlined the development of economic ties between the two countries.
According to him, bilateral trade has tripled over the past seven years. Trade turnover reached US$17.8 billion in 2025, up 34% from the previous year.
China remains Uzbekistan’s largest trading partner and its largest investor. As of September 2026, around 6,500 enterprises with Chinese capital, including joint ventures, were operating in Uzbekistan. They work in mining, agriculture, the automotive industry and other sectors.
Rakhmonov noted that Uzbekistan’s location in the centre of Central Asia offered logistical advantages. This allows joint ventures to export products to neighbouring countries and pursue business models targeting third-country markets, he said.
He expressed confidence that the exhibition would bring together advanced Chinese technologies, equipment and specialists, while giving entrepreneurs opportunities to conduct business and exchange information through electronic platforms.
He also said he expected the event to produce practical results, including the signing of memorandums and investment letters of intent by a number of companies. The ministry would actively assist Chinese enterprises in implementing projects, he added. Rakhmonov thanked the leaders of both countries and local officials for supporting bilateral relations and economic growth.
Robotics, electric vehicles and AI in focus
Liu Yue said the programme had been substantially revised from the first exhibition to better reflect the industrial profiles of China and Uzbekistan. The organisers highlighted the complementary nature of the two countries’ industries.
Key areas will include industrial automation and robotics, new-energy vehicles and components, AI-powered devices and artificial intelligence services. Other areas will feature energy storage systems, photovoltaic modules, smart-home systems, cloud computing and big data.
What visitors can expect: three key features
Liu Yue outlined three main features of the exhibition.
The indoor exhibition space will cover 4,000 square metres, while the outdoor area will exceed 800 square metres. Five themed zones will focus on intelligent manufacturing, green energy, consumer electronics, trade in services and new-energy transport.
The zones will showcase China’s progress in developing new productive forces. According to the organisers, these technologies align with the economic development and industrial modernisation priorities of Uzbekistan and other countries in the region.
For the first time, a special “China’s Opportunities” exhibition area will present the country’s progress in expanding external openness, business conditions in different regions and advanced intelligent technologies.
An interactive area dedicated to traditional Chinese culture will also be set up, allowing visitors to take part in themed activities.
The organisers aim to create an environment combining exhibition visits with interactive programmes.
Around 200 companies, more than 30% in high-tech sectors
Around 200 Chinese companies have been selected to participate. Specialised, high-tech and innovative enterprises will account for more than 30% of the participants.
The exhibitors will include CAMCE, Yonyou Network and Focus Technology, alongside companies specialising in particular fields, such as Lanxin Robotics, Zhengzhou City Unites Steel Industrial Co., Ltd. and LAISAI.
Compared with the previous exhibition, the share of companies working in artificial intelligence, energy storage and cross-border e-commerce is expected to increase significantly.
Participants will present practices in technological innovation, green and low-carbon development, and digital transformation.
The organisers expect the exhibition to support the adoption of advanced technologies and the modernisation of industrial systems across Central Asia.
Investment forum, B2B meetings and regional presentations
The exhibition is designed as a comprehensive platform combining product displays, business negotiations, service presentations and technology exchange.
The programme includes the China–Uzbekistan Investment Cooperation Forum, specialised meetings on trade and economic cooperation, and business-to-business (B2B) negotiations between companies.
Separate presentations will be held by delegations from Shaanxi Province, the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region and other Chinese regions. The organisers expect these events to connect supply and demand and facilitate targeted negotiations in specific areas.
Reaching Central Asian markets: organisers’ expectations
The organisers expect the exhibition to provide Chinese companies with a channel to enter Central Asian markets, while giving businesses in Uzbekistan and other countries in the region an opportunity to learn about China and explore new avenues for cooperation.
In their assessment, the event will give fresh impetus to the development of trade and economic ties between China and Uzbekistan and help usher in a new “golden decade” of bilateral relations.

articles.title: Azerbaijan looks to Southeast Asia to turn its transit routes into trade - AzerNews
articles.summary: Azerbaijan looks to Southeast Asia to turn its transit routes into trade  AzerNews
articles.full_text:
What business does a country on the western shore of the Caspian Sea have courting governments thousands of kilometres away in Southeast Asia?
At first glance, there seems to be little. The primary focus of Azerbaijan is in the South Caucasus region, as well as in its energy relations with Europe and the corridors through Central Asia. On the other hand, Cambodia finds itself in a market environment that is influenced by ASEAN, China, and the Pacific Ocean. But then again, that’s why their developing relationship is intriguing.
On Monday, Cambodian prime minister Hun Manet arrived in Baku for an official visit and the forthcoming summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA). His meetings with President Ilham Aliyev produced agreements on double taxation, trade and economic cooperation, and ties between diplomatic education institutions. Individually, none of them is groundbreaking. Yet collectively, they give grounds to say that Azerbaijan is experimenting with the scope of its foreign policy - possibly discovering its direction for a new era.
The idea is possibly about becoming valuable to an Asian power through providing access to its markets and transportation network, which leads to Central Asia, the Caucasus region, and ultimately Europe. It is a realistic option rather than the rhetoric of friendship, usually expressed on such occasions.
As always, Ilham Aliyev noted the discrepancies between the two countries, acknowledging the gap between political enthusiasm and commercial reality. “Our trade turnover is still very modest,” he said after the talks. The two sides established a joint working group on trade and investment, while a business forum sought to introduce companies that have had little reason to encounter one another.
In addition to geography, the president highlighted one other issue: “Another obstacle is the lack of information, and we need to close that gap.” This is an interesting revelation. Even though there has been diplomacy for well over three decades, familiarity does not mean there have been business dealings.
The agreements provide a starting point, not proof of any sort of economic breakthrough. Taxation without double taxation may simplify cross-border investments; a trade agreement may give policymakers a way to resolve such practical barriers. However, business requires customers, reasonable freight rates, dependable payments and predictable policies. The Cambodian prime minister even mentioned the idea of an agreement for air services.
The attraction of Azerbaijan for Cambodian companies may not be due to the country’s own market, but more to what it offers outside itself. According to Kith Meng, president of the Cambodian Chamber of Commerce, “there has been an interest to enter the Central Asian market through Azerbaijan.” The following are some of the topics that have been discussed during their talks.
A corridor looking for new customers
Much of Azerbaijan’s recent diplomacy has rested on the idea that geography can be converted into leverage. The Middle Corridor links China and Central Asia across the Caspian, through Azerbaijan and the South Caucasus, towards Türkiye and Europe. It is neither the only route across Eurasia nor a frictionless one. Sea crossings, border procedures and competing infrastructure priorities can all erode its commercial appeal.
Even so, the search for diversified trade routes has created an opening for countries positioned between major markets. Southeast Asian manufacturers are not about to redirect their exports wholesale through Baku. But selective cargo flows, distribution partnerships and joint ventures could make sense if the economics work. For Azerbaijan, bringing new businesses into those networks would help turn transit infrastructure into a wider commercial ecosystem. Baku, although geographically closer to Asia, has successfully established itself as a significant player in the political and economic spheres, particularly on the European side. However, many countries on the far side of the continent are still largely unaware of Azerbaijan.
In this respect, the linkage has a political nature too. For instance, Azerbaijan has tried to gain flexibility among major states without aligning its diplomacy with any particular alliance. For Azerbaijan, the engagement with Cambodia adds an Asian angle to its foreign policy, while for Cambodia, the cooperation with Azerbaijan means getting one more player who does not belong to the immediate vicinity of its bigger neighbors, as it intends to integrate its economy into the Central Asian region by developing a partnership with Azerbaijan.
Old classrooms, new forms of influence
CICA provides an institutional framework for doing so. Azerbaijan’s chairmanship, as unanimously supported by all members, according to Aliyev, and hosting of the upcoming summit will afford the opportunity to bring together governments which would otherwise have little bilateral contact. Baku and Phnom Penh already cooperate within the United Nations, the Non-Aligned Movement, and CICA.
According to Aliyev, chairmanship is a reflection of an independent policy grounded in sovereignty. This is the meaning given to it by the government, but its practical effect is access. Holding international conferences gives an opportunity to a small state to establish diplomatic contacts, put forward initiatives, and become a negotiating forum. The issue is how such contacts will lead to a durable project after the departure of delegations.
The most convincing fields for collaboration may be less spectacular than pipeline and transport projects. For instance, President Aliyev remembered how hundreds of students from Cambodia studied in Azerbaijan in Soviet times and suggested resuming educational cooperation. The cooperation between ADA University and the National Institute of Diplomacy and International Relations of Cambodia is an example.
Another form of painful experience they both share is that of land mines. They suffer the long-term consequences of contamination by explosives, and this was one of the areas where their leaders exchanged ideas about training and technology. The Azerbaijani ASAN public service model has been suggested as a potential area for collaboration. The value of such initiatives does not depend on large trade volumes. This might be the true test of Baku’s opening to Southeast Asia. One Cambodian visit alone does not make a strategic shift to the region, and there is nothing in the existing data to indicate how far along Azerbaijan is in developing a relationship with Laos or other ASEAN countries. Same initiatives, however, could be expected for Tuesday's visit of the Laos President.
But there is a serious issue behind it all. In a world where nations seek to have many friends, alternative ways, and robust connectivity, distance is not the only determinant of relevancy anymore. The idea behind the move by Azerbaijan is the expectation that a nation located between regions can actually gain importance from knowing how to connect them. It is up to the Southeast Asian business community whether they find the concept relevant enough.

articles.summary: CENTRAL ASIA ADVANCES REGIONAL TRANSPORT CONNECTIVITY AND REGULATORY HARMONISATION  EEAS
articles.full_text:
Organized by the Regional Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor Capacity Development programme, implemented by GIZ and Expertise France and co-financed by the European Union as well as the German and French Government, in cooperation with UNECE, the two-day workshop continued the regional dialogue on transport, transit and trade facilitation.
‘This important regional dialogue takes place in the context of the development of the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor (TCTC), a strategic priority for the European Union and Central Asian governments. We see that bottlenecks along this Corridor persist, and stronger regional cooperation, including on harmonisation of different trade and transport documents, is crucial for making this route reliable. It is encouraging to see how the European Union, Germany and France, working in a Team Europe approach, are able to support Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan in their better collaboration on building better and more efficient transport routes across Central Asia,’ highlighted Christos Marazopoulos, Head of Cooperation at the Delegation of the European Union to the Republic of Uzbekistan.
EUDELKZ
The discussions brought together national representatives and experts to address key issues affecting regional transport connectivity and competitiveness, including:
- Unified Railway Law (URL) and international rail transport
- Dangerous goods transport and ADR
- Harmonization of vehicle weight and dimensions
- Facilitation of international maritime transport
- Regional cooperation and the Action Plan of the Regional Working Group on Transport and Transit.
The workshop also provided an important platform for sharing national experiences and strengthening cooperation among countries of the SPECA region, with discussions highlighting the importance of coordinated approaches, regulatory harmonization and practical capacity building in supporting more efficient and predictable transport corridors.
The exchange demonstrated once again that stronger regional cooperation and alignment with international transport standards are essential to implementing the full potential of Central Asia’s role in international trade and transit.
The outcomes and discussions from the workshop will contribute to the continued regional work on transport facilitation, regulatory harmonization and the development of more efficient and competitive transport connections across Central Asia.

Amangeldiev: Kyrgyzstan Aims to Strengthen the Role of the Transport and Logistics Hub in Central Asia
Kyrgyzstan plans to strengthen its position as a central transport and logistics hub in the region, focusing on the development of international transport corridors, the construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, and expanding trade relations with foreign partners. This was announced by the First Deputy Prime Minister Daniyar Amangeldiev at the international forum "Modern Customs."
According to Amangeldiev, new opportunities for Kyrgyzstan are also opening up due to the deepening of trade and economic ties with the countries of the Eurasian Economic Union and the Turkic world.
“Kyrgyzstan aims to take a worthy place in these processes, strengthening its role as an important transport and trade-logistics hub in the region. This task is outlined in the National Development Program of the Kyrgyz Republic until 2030,” he noted.
The goal is not only to increase transit flows but also to ensure that the development of transport corridors brings tangible economic results within the country, attracts investments, creates jobs, and contributes to the development of logistics centers, warehouse infrastructure, as well as service and manufacturing enterprises.
Daniyar Amangeldiev emphasized that Kyrgyzstan must not only ensure the movement of goods but also create added value at every stage of transportation.
To achieve these goals, it is necessary not only to develop transport infrastructure but also to reduce administrative barriers, expedite border crossing processes, and ensure coordinated interaction between government agencies of different countries.
“A modern trade corridor is not just transport infrastructure, but a holistic system where the physical movement of goods is accompanied by rapid data exchange, electronic documents, advance notifications, and effective risk management. Therefore, the digital transformation of the customs system is one of our priorities,” Amangeldiev noted.

ISLAMABAD - Akramjon Nematov, First Deputy Director of the Institute for Strategic and Regional Studies under the President of Uzbekistan (ISRS), commented on the outcomes of the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, held on October 8 in the “Avaza” National Tourist Zone in Turkmenistan.
Eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, held in Avaza on October 8th, marked a fundamental shift in regional cooperation. The region is entering a new phase: from diplomacy built on trust to economic connectivity, and from resolving longstanding issues to shaping a shared future. The political trust developed in recent years is becoming a driver of tangible development, providing a foundation for joint manufacturing ventures, infrastructure and energy projects, technological cooperation, and new value chains.
Azerbaijan’s full participation significantly broadens the geographical scope and opportunities for this cooperation, strengthening Central Asia’s links with the Caspian region and the South Caucasus. Nature of regional cooperation is thus changing. Central Asia is increasingly emerging not only as a region of good-neighbourly relations and political dialogue, but also as a centre capable of shaping its own economic and technological agenda. This shift is particularly significant amid profound changes in the international system. Geopolitical tensions are reshaping established patterns of trade, transport and energy flows, reconfiguring supply chains and increasing the value of reliable connections. The technological revolution is turning data, computing capacity and skills into strategic resources, while climate change is placing growing pressure on water resources, food systems, energy and infrastructure.
As President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev noted, “The world is changing rapidly, tensions are rising, trade and transport links are being reshaped and new risks are emerging”. These conditions create a clear need for closer coordination among the countries of the region, particularly in areas where their interests and capabilities are already closely connected. Significance of the “Avaza” meeting therefore lies less in the number of proposals put forward than in the shared direction of the regional agenda, which emerged even more clearly in the statements of all six leaders.
This points to an important qualitative change: the Central Asian countries now have an agenda of their own, set their own cooperation priorities and propose mechanisms to implement them. This is an increasingly clear expression of the region’s capacity to act in its own right. Emerging model of cooperation remains open to the wider world, flexible in its arrangements and grounded in the region’s ability to determine its own priorities. President of Uzbekistan expressed its guiding philosophy clearly: “We need a flexible and transparent format in which strong, sovereign, and independent states cooperate on the basis of mutual respect, trust and pragmatism”.
Under this approach, stronger links within the region create greater opportunities for external engagement. Central Asia is increasingly positioning itself as a hub in its own right, connecting East Asia, the Caspian region, the South Caucasus, Europe, South Asia and other regions, rather than remaining on the margins of major geoeconomic developments.
Significantly, the leaders see the further development of the Consultative Meetings primarily in terms of effectiveness and the delivery of agreed commitments. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev advocated preserving the format as a platform for direct dialogue and proposed taking stock of earlier regional initiatives. The President of Uzbekistan expressed a similar view: “The number of documents in itself does not solve much. What matters far more is that the decisions we have already taken are implemented and deliver the results they were intended to achieve”.
The next phase of cooperation will therefore involve strengthening implementation mechanisms, improving coordination among the relevant agencies and consistently following through on agreements, while preserving the flexibility and trust that define the format. The aim is to establish institutional arrangements that make cooperation more effective without making it more cumbersome.
Convergence of interests was particularly evident in the economic sphere. Kazakhstan proposed increasing intraregional trade and linking trade and logistics hubs with centres for industrial cooperation to create regional value chains. Kyrgyzstan focused on specific projects in agricultural processing, light industry, building materials and logistics. Tajikistan emphasised joint ventures, industrial complexes and manufacturing and export projects. Azerbaijan proposed making greater use of existing joint investment funds to establish new manufacturing operations and enter international markets. Turkmenistan also identified industrial, investment, transport and energy cooperation as key priorities.
Against this background, the formula proposed by the President of Uzbekistan, “six economies – one product”, builds naturally on this common direction. It seeks to complement mutual trade with deeper collaboration in manufacturing, bringing together the resources, technologies, capital, industrial capacity, skills and logistics of several countries to produce finished goods.
This reveals another fundamental shift. The region is gradually moving beyond a role centred primarily on transit and raw materials, and is demonstrating its readiness to become an important link in global manufacturing value chains. This strengthens the resilience of national economies, broadens market access for businesses and places economic connectivity on a firmer footing.
Uzbekistan’s proposals for a Central Asia–Azerbaijan Business Forum in Khiva and a Platform for Financial and Technical Support of Joint Investment Projects offer practical ways to advance this approach. They would provide the tools for project preparation, expert assessment, financial structuring and implementation support needed to turn political commitments to industrial cooperation into results. Uzbekistan’s initiatives thus build on priorities already identified by its partners and help translate them into investment and manufacturing projects.
A similar complementarity is evident in transport. Kyrgyzstan sees the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway as central to future opportunities and proposes assessing transport projects by delivery costs and journey times. Kazakhstan is expanding the capacity of the Middle Corridor and the North–South route. Azerbaijan is steadily developing the Caspian link and the Trans-Caspian route. Tajikistan is focusing on multimodal transport, the removal of administrative barriers and the digitalization of procedures. Turkmenistan is developing connections along the East–West and North–South axes.
In this context, the President of Uzbekistan’s proposal to accelerate the establishment of the Council for Infrastructure Development advances the shared objective of connecting transport projects. Such a mechanism could help coordinate the development of roads, railways, ports, border infrastructure and logistics centres, integrating individual national routes into a more coherent regional network.
Transport connectivity is understood to extend well beyond the movement of goods. The development of corridors creates opportunities for new manufacturing facilities, industrial zones, logistics hubs and service facilities along their routes. Infrastructure thus becomes a driver of both territorial development and value creation.
This approach offers a new perspective on Central Asia’s place in Eurasia’s emerging connectivity network. The China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway, the infrastructure of Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan’s Caspian transport capacity and Tajikistan’s multimodal transport capabilities are gradually forming a broader network of interregional connections.
Central Asia is thus emerging as a potential key pillar of this connectivity network, linking different markets and routes while strengthening its own manufacturing and logistics capacity.
A similar trend is emerging in energy. Tajikistan proposed drawing up a list of priority energy projects, identifying mechanisms for their joint financing and developing a regional strategy for the green transition. Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are already working to establish a green energy corridor across the Caspian Sea. Turkmenistan likewise considers energy one of the key areas for expanded cooperation.
Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s proposed Joint Concept for Low-Carbon Energy Potential takes this shared agenda forward through systematic planning. It would allow new generation capacity, energy storage and energy corridors to be planned around the complementary roles of hydrocarbons, hydropower, solar and wind generation. National energy strengths could thereby be combined more systematically into a resilient regional system.
Important areas of common interest are also emerging in the digital sector. Azerbaijan is developing Digital Silk Way and trans-Caspian fibre-optic infrastructure. articles.title: Central Asian Leaders Espouse Unity, But Stop Short Of Backing Words With Action - Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Central Asian Leaders Espouse Unity, But Stop Short Of Backing Words With Action - Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- At the 8th Consultative Meeting of Central Asian leaders and Azerbaijan, the C6 states pledged closer coordination on trade, transport and security, with host Turkmenistan unusually committing to break from isolationism and support a unified approach.
- Leaders elevated the long-stalled trans-Caspian pipeline and the Central Asia–Caspian–Europe corridor as priorities, while Uzbekistan floated a regional skills atlas and both Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan pressed for joint mechanisms to manage scarce transboundary water resources, including dialogue with Afghanistan.
- The joint statement remained largely aspirational, so progress on a water convention or standing professional-standards body before the 2027 meeting will test whether the group moves beyond rhetoric.
(Eurasianet) — The heads of C6 states, comprising the five Central Asian nations and Azerbaijan, said all the right things at their most recent conclave concerning a desire for more economic cooperation. All eyes will now be on them to give practical meaning to their words.
Participants at the 8th Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, were unanimous on October 8 in articulating needs for closer coordination in such areas as trade, transport and regional security, according to a joint statement issued after the meeting.
Perhaps most significant, the host nation, Turkmenistan, affirmed its readiness to break out of its historically isolationist shell and join neighboring states in building the infrastructure needed to expand trade and promote the digitalization of regional economies. Given Turkmenistan’s traditional policy of neutrality, Turkmen President Serdar Berdymukhamedov’s welcoming address was unusually jargon-free and contained an extraordinary (for Ashgabat) call for a unified approach in addressing key issues.
Berdymukhamedov indicated that a top diplomatic priority for Turkmenistan would be fulfilling the “potential of the six-party partnership, preserving and strengthening the spirit of solidarity, unity and mutual support.”
He also expressed hope that the consultative meeting would “inject new momentum into trade, economic and investment cooperation, and to pool efforts to transform Central Asia and Azerbaijan into key and indispensable participants in … transport, logistics, energy and industrial corridors.”
The meeting’s joint statement made clear that construction of a trans-Caspian pipeline, long stalled by a variety of factors, is now high on the C6 agenda. Ashgabat, which has historically held a fickle position on the pipeline, signaled that it is fully on board with the project
Berdymukhamedov issued a call for “maximum substance to be given to negotiations and actions to create transport and logistics connectivity,” adding that “the Central Asia–Caspian Sea–South Caucasus–Europe corridor is expected to play a key role here.”
Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev was among those urging the creation of institutions and value chains to address trade and development challenges. “We need a flexible and transparent format in which strong, sovereign and independent states cooperate on the basis of mutual respect, trust and pragmatism,” he said. “We have already set ambitious goals for increasing mutual trade and investment. Now it is necessary to determine what will drive this growth.”
Among the ideas that Mirziyoyev floated was the creation of a Regional Atlas of In-Demand Professions and Skills to help governments ensure the region’s available labor pool is trained up to meet development needs in such sectors as mining, tourism and AI/IT.
The issue of conserving dwindling regional water resources received a lot of attention during the meeting. Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev indicated that hitting the economic development targets of each C6 state depends heavily on the countries’ ability to jointly ensure adequate water supplies for industrial and household use.
“We face the task of developing new approaches to the management of transboundary water resources,” Tokayev told his fellow leaders. “The adoption of a Central Asian Framework Convention on Water Use could serve as a starting point for shaping a new regional architecture of cooperation. This draft document is already under consideration by all parties.”
Mirziyoyev, meanwhile, proposed the establishment of a standing body to facilitate “dialogue with Afghanistan on water resource use, taking into account the interests of all countries in the region.”
Those and other ideas were not reflected in the joint statement, which was largely limited to aspirational concepts. Whether C6 leaders adopt a framework water convention or establish a regional mechanism to raise professional standards before the next C6 gathering in 2027 will provide a gauge of their determination to move beyond rhetoric and work toward a regional grouping of states.

articles.title: Why Belgium’s royal visit to Kazakhstan matters beyond diplomacy - EUalive
articles.summary: Why Belgium’s royal visit to Kazakhstan matters beyond diplomacy  EUalive

Belgium’s King Philippe and Queen Mathilde will make their first state visit to Kazakhstan on 11-14 October, bringing a high-level government, business and academic delegation to talks on critical minerals, transport routes, health care and artificial intelligence as the two countries seek to expand economic ties.
The visit, the first Belgian state visit to Central Asia, comes as Europe looks to diversify critical raw material supplies and strengthen transport links with the region. For Kazakhstan, closer ties with Belgium offer access to European technology, investment and logistics expertise as Astana works to broaden its economic partnerships and reduce its dependence on traditional export routes.
The royal couple will visit Astana, where they are scheduled to meet President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, before travelling to Almaty. They will be accompanied by a 110-member delegation, including senior Belgian government officials, 25 business executives and academic representatives. The foreign ministries are also expected to sign a 2026-2029 roadmap, according to an official government release, and the fourth meeting of the Kazakh-Belgian Business Council is also scheduled.
“It will provide an opportunity to highlight success stories and explore new forms of cooperation in logistics and agriculture, two areas in which Belgium and Kazakhstan already enjoy close collaboration,” reads Belgium’s official government release.
Philippe previously visited Kazakhstan three times as crown prince, in 2002, 2009 and 2010. This will be his first visit as king. As a crown prince, he travelled to Baikonur cosmodrome in 2002 and 2009 for the launches of Belgian astronaut Frank De Winne’s missions to the International Space Station. He returned in 2010 to lead an economic mission to the country. The royal visit also reflects a broader effort by Kazakhstan to strengthen European partnerships as geopolitical tensions reshape trade routes, investment decisions and access to strategic resources.
President Tokayev paid an official visit to Brussels in November 2021, which was his first official visit to Europe since the pandemic and his first to Belgium as the country’s president. He also travelled to Brussels in June and Berlin and Munich in September this year, underscoring Astana’s efforts to translate closer political relations into investment, trade and industrial cooperation.
“In the face of current geopolitical challenges, Belgium intends to diversify its partnerships and strengthen its presence in a region that offers significant strategic opportunities. It wishes to deepen its cooperation with Kazakhstan, in order to build a more sustainable, resilient and prosperous future together,” reads an official Belgium government release.
What do the two countries trade Belgium’s trade with Kazakhstan has also grown over the past several years, although the latest figures show uneven momentum. Bilateral trade reached $582.4 million in 2025, up nearly 28% from the previous year, according to the Kazakh government. Kazakhstan exported $311.5 million in goods to Belgium and imported $270.9 million.
Kazakhstan is also an important Central Asian market for Belgian exporters. Figures from the Belgian Foreign Trade Agency show that Belgian goods exports to Kazakhstan in 2025 were nearly five times those to either Uzbekistan or the Kyrgyz Republic. Within the European Union, Belgium ranked seventh among exporters of goods to Kazakhstan in 2025, accounting for 5.7% of the bloc’s 10.6 billion euros (US$11.9 billion) in exports. It ranked 14th among EU importers of Kazakh goods, with a 0.5% share of the EU’s approximately 30.9 billion euros (US$34.6 billion) in imports.
The two countries trade largely different products. Pharmaceuticals lead Belgium’s exports to Kazakhstan. Chemical and pharmaceutical products, primarily medicines, immunological products and vaccines, accounted for 48.4% of Belgian goods exports in 2025, worth 292.5 million euros (US$327.8 million). Machinery and equipment, along with transport equipment, were also among the leading export categories. Kazakhstan’s exports to Belgium remain concentrated in a handful of commodities. Vegetable products, primarily linseed, accounted for 46.2% of Belgian goods imports from Kazakhstan, worth 74.6 million euros (US$83.6 million). Mineral products, largely molybdenum ores and concentrates, followed at 61.1 million euros (US$64.5 million), or 37.9%. Base metals, including ferroalloys and refined copper, made up another 8.8%.
Belgium has also been a substantial source of foreign investment in Kazakhstan, with gross foreign direct investment inflows exceeding $14 billion between 2005 and 2025, including $1.045 billion last year. To facilitate trade cooperation, Belgium established a Trade Office AWEX in Almaty in 2007. In 2021, a Chamber of Commerce for the countries of Benelux, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxemburg, was launched.
“Kazakhstan and Belgium have significant potential to expand cooperation, particularly in investment, transport and logistics, industry and technology. For Kazakhstan, Belgium is not only an economic partner in its own right but also a major industrial, financial and logistics hub within the European Union,” Alisher Abdreshev, a lead expert in the Department for European and American Studies at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, told The Astana Times. He sees Kazakhstan’s appeal extending beyond its domestic market. “Kazakhstan can offer Belgian businesses an integrated platform for industrial production, logistics and access to the wider Eurasian market,” he said.
Agricultural processing offers one potential avenue for moving beyond commodity trade. In August, Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry reported talks with Belgian companies Maselis Group and Borlix NV on food ingredients, processing and possible investment projects. Critical minerals: moving beyond raw material exports Critical minerals are also expected to feature prominently in the discussions, reflecting Europe’s efforts to diversify its supplies of materials essential for clean energy technologies, electronics and advanced manufacturing. Kazakhstan says it has 21 of the 34 raw materials identified as critical by the European Union.
“Belgium, meanwhile, has a well-developed chemical industry, advanced metallurgical technologies and expertise in materials processing. This creates opportunities to move beyond trade in raw materials toward joint manufacturing projects that generate greater added value,” said Abdreshev. “Potential areas of cooperation include metals processing, industrial component manufacturing and the development of resilient supply chains serving European markets. Such partnerships would support Kazakhstan’s efforts to diversify its economy while aligning with the European Union’s goal of diversifying its sources of strategic raw materials,” he explained.
The two countries have explored cooperation in sustainable metallurgy and critical raw materials through Belgian research institutions, including KU Leuven. The cooperation also aligns with the strategic partnership on sustainable raw materials, batteries and renewable hydrogen that Kazakhstan and the EU established in 2022. Transport connectivity Transport and logistics are another priority as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its position along trade routes connecting Asia and Europe. Kazakhstan’s Caspian ports of Aktau and Kuryk, which form part of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, could open opportunities for Belgian logistics companies seeking access to Central Asian and Chinese markets, Abdreshev said.
One of the companies with ongoing projects is Jan De Nul, a major Belgian family-owned engineering and construction company specializing in dredging, marine and port infrastructure, offshore energy and complex engineering projects. The expert also pointed to Kazakhstan’s existing investment infrastructure and experience working with European companies.
“Kazakhstan is seeking Belgian technology and management expertise to develop the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor. The Port of Antwerp-Bruges, one of Europe’s largest logistics hubs, could play a key role in these efforts. Its expertise in digitalizing port operations, multimodal transport and cargo management could help modernize Kazakhstan’s ports of Aktau and Kuryk,” said Abdreshev.
Technology, health care and academic cooperation
The royal visit is also expected to advance cooperation in artificial intelligence and health care. During Tokayev’s June visit to Brussels, Kazakhstan signed cooperation agreements with Ghent University and KU Leuven covering joint research, academic exchanges and technological development.
One of them brought together the Serikbayev East Kazakhstan technical University, KU Leuven and the SIM2 KU Leuven Institute for Sustainable Metals and Minerals, along with Astana Hub. The Ghent University partnership focused on establishing a mirror research laboratory in Kazakhstan focused on mathematical modeling, scientific computing, digital twins and AI. The agreements provide a foundation for further collaboration between Kazakh and Belgian universities, including research projects linked to European scientific programs.
Health care is another established area of economic cooperation, given Belgium’s strong pharmaceutical exports to Kazakhstan. The visit could provide opportunities to explore further cooperation in medical technologies, pharmaceutical production and research.
“The greatest potential for Kazakhstan-Belgium cooperation therefore lies in moving beyond traditional trade toward deeper investment and technological partnerships. Belgium could become an important partner in Kazakhstan’s efforts to modernize its industries and expand access to European markets.
