articles.title: Is All Foreign Policy Local? Explaining Georgia’s Shifting Alignments - Civil Georgia
articles.summary: Is All Foreign Policy Local? Explaining Georgia’s Shifting Alignments  Civil Georgia
articles.full_text:
The ruling Georgian Dream (GD) party has turned increasingly authoritarian over the past few years. Faced with a worsening security environment, local legitimacy concerns, and growing international isolation, the party increasingly tied its foreign policy alignment choices to its domestic needs. It nourished the relationships that boosted its legitimacy and contested those that threatened its domestic rule.
Several foreign policy alignment patterns emerged as a result. First, Georgian ruling elites abandoned the West as a balancing option against Russia, instead seeing its former partnerships as principal threats to regime survival. Secondly, it chose security bandwagoning with Russia, along with economic accommodation meant to further aid regime survival. Third is transactional and legitimacy-enhancing engagements with the rest of the world — primarily with China, but also with states in the immediate neighborhood and beyond.
While GD seems to have so far managed to retain power, it has yet to achieve the ideal multi-aligned state it claims to pursue. The European Union (EU) keeps resisting Tbilisi’s calls to engage without democratic conditionality; the U.S. has yet to clearly respond to Tbilisi’s calls for a reset; bandwagoning with Russia has hit clear limits amid the continued occupation of Georgian regions; and relations with the rest of the world, including China, have served as legitimacy-enhancers rather than achieving genuine strategic depth.
More alarmingly, however, this search risks undermining the country’s foreign policy autonomy, limiting its room for geopolitical maneuver amidst the global uncertainty.
Authors: Irakli Sirbiladze, Tamta Bezhanishvili, and Luka Danelia
Georgia’s Past Alignments
Georgia has often defied ideal-type foreign policy alignment categories such as bandwagoning, balancing, neutrality, or hedging. After initial bandwagoning with Moscow in the early 1990s, Georgia has embraced growing alignment with the West. Facing Russian threats and lacking internal capabilities, the country has pursued a NATO membership goal to balance against Moscow. This balancing behavior persisted despite Russia’s aggression in 2008 and a continued absence of Western security shelter.
Since coming to power in 2012, Georgian Dream has embraced both bandwagoning and balancing strategies. Even while seeking economic normalization with Russia and avoiding escalatory language, the memories of war and continued occupation of its territories limited the extent to which Tbilisi could bandwagon with Moscow. Balancing logic has persisted as the GD continued political and military cooperation with the West.
Georgian Dream chose regime survival over consolidating democracy and pursuing Georgia’s Western integration.
That changed with Russia’s full-scale aggression on Ukraine in 2022, which altered the Georgian Dream calculus. To navigate international constraints and weakening domestic legitimacy, the party hardened its bandwagoning with Moscow while softening its strategy to balance against Russia through the West. Tbilisi also sought political partnerships beyond Russia and the West, with a multi-alignment strategy in mind to hedge against uncertainties.
What remained certain, however, was that Russia was still the principal threat to the country’s security, leaving Georgia moving back and forth between bandwagoning and balancing options.
Changing Alignments in Changing Context
In the years that followed, Georgian Dream’s foreign policy alignment choices came to reflect changing domestic and international environments.
At home, Georgian Dream has faced an acute legitimacy crisis amid growing autocratization and an anti-Western turn. Internationally, Russian revisionism forced Georgian Dream to make a choice between accommodating or contesting Moscow. The EU’s revived enlargement policy, which links accession progress to democratic reforms, threatened Georgian Dream’s hold on power. The party’s response featured more Westlessness in foreign policy, a hardened bandwagoning with Russia, and an increased engagement with actors beyond Russia and the West.
- West(-lessness): From a balancing partner to a political threat
Georgian Dream’s autocratization and the Ukraine war context have strained Tbilisi’s close ties with the EU and the US.
The relationship with the EU is now at its historic low. Georgian Dream’s stark disregard of the EU’s democratic conditionality since 2022 has resulted in a frozen accession process and the suspension of high-level political dialogue between Tbilisi and Brussels in 2024. The political ties with individual EU member states and the UK also suffered. Georgian Dream kept accusing Brussels of domestic meddling and of pushing the country into war with Russia.
The partnership with Washington has been similarly tainted. In response to Georgian Dream’s growing assault on democracy, the Biden administration has imposed sanctions on the ruling party’s billionaire founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, and suspended the strategic partnership with the country late in 2024. The Trump administration has not so far reversed the Biden-era decisions. In parallel, the Trump administration’s peace agenda between Armenia and Azerbaijan has taken Georgia out of the geopolitical spotlight, despite Washington’s limited engagement with Tbilisi on connectivity projects and security.
Georgia stands as a cautionary reminder that when ruling elites fail to uphold a geopolitical balancing act in a fractured international order, the gradual loss of a country’s autonomy could be the ultimate price.
Attempts to fundamentally refresh ties with the U.S. have yet to bear fruit: while the past year saw revived contacts between Tbilisi and Washington, those visits also demonstrated that the aspired “reset” came with its conditions: the Trump administration requested political stability underpinned by political pluralism and a friendly environment for American business, clashing with the Georgian Dream’s autocratic agenda. While the launch of the Trump Tower project in Tbilisi shows Georgian Dream seeking a transactional bargain with Trump, its bearing on official Washington’s policy toward Georgia remains unknown.
Georgia’s broader foreign policy and security alignment with the West similarly suffered. Tbilisi’s alignment rate with the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) is in decline while its participation in the EU’s international missions has been suspended since 2023. Georgia no longer receives EU defense support, and the country remains outside the emerging European security architecture. Although limited defense and security cooperation with Washington and NATO continues, the scale and scope of practical cooperation is significantly downgraded. This leaves Georgia without a balancing partner or a potential European security shelter against growing Russian threats.
- Russia: security bandwagoning with economic benefits
The Ukraine war led Georgian Dream to embrace a hardened security bandwagon with Russia. The party’s leadership has consistently declared that they are staying militarily out of the war and refused to impose bilateral economic sanctions on Russia. They also abstained from deepening security cooperation with the West. GD chose to stay under the radar instead of taking full advantage of emerging security thinking in the West.
This accommodating posture with Moscow came with its economic perks. Georgian Dream deepened its trade and economic ties with Moscow and refused to close airspace to Russian air companies. The Georgian economy benefited from the growing influx of Russian immigrants. Georgia has experienced strong economic growth during 2022-2025, allowing the ruling party to govern amid suspended Western financial support.
At the same time, while remaining formally compliant with Western sanctions imposed on Russia, Tbilisi kept drawing scrutiny by drastically increasing Russian oil imports and faced allegations of refining it to export it to the outside world. The scrutiny led to the conditional inclusion of the Kulevi Oil Refinery in the EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia.
In a turbulent and transitional world order, small states face a difficult task of pursuing balanced relationships with all competing powers to maintain both security and autonomy. Driven by party interests, Georgian Dream leadership is failing the task.
Georgian Dream also followed Kremlin narratives in contesting the West. While the party has formally and selectively endorsed resolutions supporting Ukraine, it has waged persistent anti-Western disinformation campaigns mirroring Russian disinformation narratives and portraying the West as undergoing an economic and identity crisis. Georgian Dream’s consistent use of conspiracy theories – including the instrumentalization of the peace narrative – to manipulate domestic audiences has amplified Russia’s own anti-Western agenda. The party’s recent campaign to “nip Russophobia in the bud” not only mirrors the Kremlin’s talking points, but also exposes the country to Russia’s future claims of “defending” its citizens living in Georgia.
Still, the history of the 2008 war, ongoing Russian occupation, and Moscow’s recognition of Georgian regions as “independent states,” coupled with persistent anti-Russia and pro-Western attitudes among Georgians, tie Georgian Dream’s hands in pursuing a full political thaw with Moscow. The party has refrained from restoring diplomatic relations with Russia or joining the 3+3 initiative, which excludes the West and brings Turkey, Russia, and Iran together with South Caucasus states.
The Georgian Dream leadership acknowledges the political costs of formalizing ties with Moscow, as a confident majority of Georgians continue to support EU integration and see Russia as a political threat. These constraints and regime survival calculations thus force the Georgian Dream to value the status quo over an open political tilt toward Moscow.
- Beyo

President Tokayev personally welcomed the royal couple at the airport, where an honor guard was assembled for their arrival. King Philippe and Queen Mathilde arrived aboard an aircraft operated by Kazakhstan's Air Astana airline.
The royal couple is accompanied by a 110-member delegation consisting of ministers, business leaders, university rectors and journalists. The state visit will take place from October 11 to 14 and marks the royal couple's first state visit to a Central Asian country.
Following their arrival, President Tokayev held a brief conversation with King Philippe and Queen Mathilde in the airport's arrival hall. During the conversation, Tokayev emphasized the significance of the visit for strengthening relations between Kazakhstan and Belgium.
King Philippe thanked the Kazakh president for the reception and expressed confidence in the outcome of the upcoming talks, noting their importance for developing cooperation between the two countries.
The official program of the state visit will begin on October 12 with a welcoming ceremony at Akorda, followed by extended-format talks and a lunch. The royal couple will then visit the National Center for Children's Rehabilitation in Astana, which provides services in speech therapy, Montessori education and robotics. The visit is related to Queen Mathilde's background in speech therapy, which she previously studied. The day will conclude with a state dinner.
On October 13, King Philippe and Queen Mathilde will visit the National Museum of Kazakhstan, where they will tour exhibitions dedicated to Kazakh history and traditions. The program also includes the opening of an exhibition featuring works by Belgian painter James Ensor. The delegation will then attend a roundtable discussion on critical minerals at Nazarbayev University, which maintains cooperation with Belgian universities.
The royal couple will also participate in the opening of the Kazakh-Belgian Business Council. Officials will attend the opening session, while the council's activities will continue throughout the afternoon.
The delegation will subsequently visit the Alem.ai International Center for Artificial Intelligence, where the royal couple will tour TUMO Astana and meet students. Ghent University will donate a telescope to the center for use in student research. The center will also host a forum of university rectors focusing on artificial intelligence in research and education.
The event is being held in connection with Kazakhstan's designation of 2026 as the Year of Artificial Intelligence. The program in Astana will conclude with a Belgian reception in the evening.
On October 14, King Philippe, Queen Mathilde and the accompanying delegation will travel to Almaty. The delegation will visit the Institute of Nuclear Physics, which cooperates with two Belgian companies and a Belgian university. Following a cultural activity, the visit will conclude at the Almaty Museum of Arts with a dance performance by a choreographer who trained in Belgium.
The royal couple and the accompanying delegation will then depart for Belgium.

articles.title: Zelensky doubtful on Russian acceptance of Trump's 'energy ceasefire' - zeta.com.pa
articles.summary: Zelensky doubtful on Russian acceptance of Trump's 'energy ceasefire'  zeta.com.pa
articles.full_text:
Compartir:
12 October 2026
Kyiv (Ukraine) (AFP) -
Russia does not want to accept an 'energy ceasefire' in Ukraine announced by Donald Trump, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, accusing Moscow of attacking six sites Monday.
Zelensky earlier promised to respond if Russia refused to agree to the truce, as Moscow indicated it would not adhere to the US president's calls for a pause in attacks on power infrastructure.
Trump sowed confusion on Sunday with a surprise announcement on his Truth Social network that there was an agreement on both sides to end their punishing long-range strikes on power plants and oil refineries.
'It is increasingly evident that Russia is unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire proposed by the United States,' Zelensky said on social media.
'Today alone, the Russians have attacked six energy facilities in Ukraine. Thirty-three people were wounded across the country,' he added.
Zelensky had said Ukraine would back the ceasefire.
'If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,' he told the Warsaw Security Conference.
Moscow has refused to say if an 'energy ceasefire' was in place and appeared to reject Zelensky's offer of a 60-day pause in hostilities for elections to be held in Ukraine -- which both the Kremlin and the White House have demanded.
'We don't want a ceasefire, we want long-term peace,' Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters, saying President Vladimir Putin would only order his troops to cease fire on election day itself.
'I do not think he (Zelensky) deserves a respite,' added Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.
- Real deal -
Ukraine's Western allies have all backed a pause in attacks targeting the energy sector, as Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II nears its fifth anniversary and winter approaches.
But they have lined up to condemn Trump's announcement to allow Russia to supply diesel exports, with gas prices surging before US midterm elections next month and Trump's Republicans expected to be hit hard.
On Monday, the European Union formally added almost 1,600 new individuals and entities to its lengthy sanctions list to further turn the screws on Russia and its war machine.
Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Europe would not go soft on Russia and that Moscow 'will only negotiate seriously under pressure'.
Zelensky said Ukraine was awaiting specific details of Trump's purported deal but said security guarantees were needed 'here in reality, not just on Truth Social'.
A 13-year-old girl was among three generations of the same family who were killed in a Russian strike near the frontline city of Kramatorsk on Monday, the authorities said.
The head of the military administration in the Donetsk region, Vadym Filashkin, accused Russian forces of using cluster munitions in 'a deliberate attempt to inflict as many casualties as possible among civilians'.
Last week, 30 people were killed when a Russian strike hit two buses in Kramatorsk.
- 'Dominance' -
Putin claims the Donetsk region as a whole and has previously rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky, making European leaders sceptical about whether he would accept any temporary pause in the bitter fighting.
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk told the Warsaw conference that Moscow was 'not interested in a ceasefire or in de-escalation or peace'.
'It is interested only in domination,' he said, urging European and US unity to ensure Ukraine's 'survival' against Russia's attempts for 'dominance'.
NATO's top military commander, US General Alexus Grynkewich, told the conference that the alliance would 'block, blunt and break' any Russian attempt to attack its members, as fears grow about the threat from Moscow.
Even after Trump's announcement, Ukraine reported a Russian drone attack on a gas facility in the eastern Kharkiv region, which operator Naftogaz said damaged 'critical equipment' and forced emergency repairs.
Russia has previously attacked Ukraine's energy sector before winter, leaving many Ukrainians without power or heating as temperatures dropped as low as -20C.
According to Green Deal Ukraine, an expert group, Ukraine's power generation capacity was 39.5 gigawatts just before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
But that had plunged to 13.5 GW in September this year.

articles.title: Tokayev, King Philippe Pledge to Deepen Kazakhstan-Belgium Ties in Joint Statement - The Astana Times
articles.summary: Tokayev, King Philippe Pledge to Deepen Kazakhstan-Belgium Ties in Joint Statement  The Astana Times
articles.full_text:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Belgium reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations, focusing on the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, artificial intelligence, critical minerals and cooperation on international topics, according to a joint statement adopted by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and King Philippe of the Belgians on Oct. 12.
The statement followed talks during the Belgian royal couple’s state visit to Kazakhstan on Oct. 11-14, which both officials described as an important milestone in bilateral relations.
Middle Corridor and digital technologies
The two countries underscored the growing role of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or Middle Corridor, as a reliable and sustainable transport link between Asia and Europe.
They also reaffirmed the importance of developing transport and logistics cooperation and enhancing connectivity between the two regions.
Digitalization, artificial intelligence and innovation were identified as increasingly important for sustainable economic development and competitiveness. The two leaders expressed interest in developing cooperation in artificial intelligence, big data, cloud technologies, supercomputing infrastructure and data centers.
During the press briefing, Tokayev highlighted Kazakhstan’s interest in expanding cooperation across emerging industries, including digitalization and space technologies.
King Philippe, in turn, underlined Kazakhstan’s technological development, noting that the country was “at the forefront of digitalization” and had developed unique solutions, notably in artificial intelligence.
“We are keen to visit the Alem.AI center and discuss synergies between our countries,” he said.
Critical minerals and economic cooperation
The joint statement reaffirmed the importance of cooperation in critical minerals, petrochemicals, industry and mechanical engineering, and renewable energy.
The leaders welcomed the holding of a roundtable on critical minerals during the state visit, underscoring the strategic importance of cooperation in this field.
They also highlighted the potential to expand agricultural trade, develop the food industry and introduce modern agricultural technologies.
Tokayev noted that Belgium had invested more than $15 billion in Kazakhstan’s economy since 2005, describing economic cooperation as a cornerstone of bilateral relations.
The leaders welcomed the Kazakhstan-Belgium Business Council’s activities and the fourth meeting during the visit as an important mechanism for strengthening ties between the two countries’ business communities.
The statement also reaffirmed their commitment to the Enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreement between Kazakhstan and the European Union and its member states, signed on Dec. 21, 2015.
Education, healthcare and cultural ties
The two officials welcomed the Kazakhstan-Belgium Rectors’ Forum and expressed support for joint educational programs, academic mobility, scientific research and partnerships between universities and research centers.
They also reaffirmed the importance of strengthening healthcare cooperation, including enhancing the role of primary healthcare within the World Health Organization Global Coalition for Primary Health Care.
The leaders referred to the principles of the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration on Primary Health Care and the 2018 Astana Declaration, as well as initiatives to be discussed following the conference Towards the 50th Anniversary of the Alma-Ata Declaration: Building Strong Primary Health Care for Future Generations, scheduled for Oct. 14 in Almaty.
The discussions also featured cultural cooperation. Tokayev welcomed the presentation of works by Belgian artist James Ensor at Kazakhstan’s National Museum and cooperation between the Almaty Museum of Arts and KANAL-Center Pompidou.
Tokayev and King Philippe further welcomed the entry into force of the protocol amending the agreement between Kazakhstan and the Benelux countries on visa exemption for holders of service passports.
They also expressed their intention to conclude negotiations and sign a bilateral agreement on remunerated employment for family members of diplomatic missions as a deliverable marking 35 years of diplomatic relations between Kazakhstan and Belgium in 2027.
Commitment to international law and dialogue
On international and regional matters, the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to multilateralism, international law and the United Nations’ central role in maintaining international peace and security, promoting sustainable development and addressing global challenges.
They agreed to intensify bilateral political dialogue on international affairs and economic development within the United Nations, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), and multilateral platforms in the Kazakhstan-EU and Central Asia-EU formats.
The statement also highlighted the importance of strengthening the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production and Stockpiling of Bacteriological (Biological) and Toxin Weapons and on Their Destruction, adopted on April 10, 1972.
The leaders expressed satisfaction with the outcomes of their talks and reaffirmed their determination to give new impetus to the Kazakhstan-Belgium partnership.
Both officials expressed confidence that King Philippe’s first state visit to Kazakhstan would lay the foundation for the further qualitative development of bilateral relations.

articles.title: Brazilian Expert Says Kazakhstan’s Foreign Policy Offers Lessons for Brazil - The Astana Times
articles.summary: Brazilian Expert Says Kazakhstan’s Foreign Policy Offers Lessons for Brazil  The Astana Times
articles.full_text:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s balanced foreign policy, advances in artificial intelligence and institutional reforms offer valuable lessons for Brazil, while cooperation in critical minerals, energy and logistics could strengthen ties between the two countries, said Márcio Coimbra, director of Casa Política and president of the Monitor da Democracia Institute, in an interview with The Astana Times.
Coimbra is visiting Central Asia for the first time, with plans to travel to the Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan before continuing to the Caucasus. He said the region’s rapid development and growing geopolitical importance deserve greater attention in Latin America.
“But it’s a part of the world that Latin America doesn’t look at with the right attention. And it calls my attention because it’s becoming very developed very fast here,” he said.
Kazakhstan’s balanced diplomacy offers lessons for Brazil
Coimbra identified Kazakhstan’s ability to maintain constructive relations with major global powers as one of the country’s most valuable experiences for Brazil.
Coimbra said Brazil could learn from Kazakhstan’s foreign policy approach, notably its emphasis on national sovereignty and economic interests.
“I’ve always defended that Brazil needs to be defending Brazil’s sovereignty. And I think that you do it in a very smart way here,” he said.
He described Kazakhstan’s approach as balancing Beijing, Brussels and Washington while prioritizing national economic interests.
“Because then you put your economic interests first and Kazakhstan first,” he said.
Coimbra said Brazil could apply similar principles to its own foreign policy. He also emphasized the need to strengthen ties between Brazil and Kazakhstan, which share challenges and opportunities as middle powers.
Cooperation in critical minerals, AI and energy
Coimbra highlighted critical minerals, artificial intelligence, renewable energy and agriculture as promising areas for bilateral cooperation.
Both countries possess substantial natural resources, including critical minerals, but face challenges in developing domestic processing capacity. He noted that China remains a major processor of rare earth elements, creating opportunities for countries to diversify supply chains and develop their own industrial capabilities.
He also pointed to Kazakhstan’s progress in artificial intelligence, including the development of data centers and a large language model based on its national language.
Brazil’s extensive hydropower resources could support cooperation in digital infrastructure. Coimbra said Kazakhstan and Brazil could explore partnerships connecting Kazakhstan’s data center ambitions with Brazil’s clean electricity supply.
He also identified opportunities in oil and gas expertise, agricultural production and logistics, including connections between Kazakhstan’s Middle Corridor and Latin American trade flows.
“Things that are missing to you are in Brazil. And things that are missing in Brazil you have here,” he said.
Reforms should reflect national values
Coimbra welcomed Kazakhstan’s institutional reforms, including the transition to a unicameral parliament and the introduction of the Kurultai, describing them as steps toward a political system rooted in the country’s history and culture.
He said countries should develop institutions suited to their own circumstances rather than simply importing foreign models.
“Every country has the right to find its own system that adapts to its own culture,” he said.
Turning potential into practical partnerships
Despite shared economic interests, Coimbra said geographic distance, limited direct air connections and a lack of information have constrained relations between Central Asia and Latin America.
He noted that reaching Kazakhstan from Brazil involves multiple flight connections, making travel more difficult and expensive. He said stronger transport links would help bring the regions closer together.
Coimbra called for stronger business links, targeted investment projects, technology transfer and more structured cooperation between the two countries’ private sectors.
He also proposed leveraging multilateral platforms, including the United Nations, the G20 and BRICS, to align positions on sustainable development and global governance.
“The single largest opportunity lies in creating a strategic commodity and infrastructural bridge,” he said, emphasizing the need to move beyond broad agreements toward practical, co-financed projects.
For Coimbra, stronger Kazakhstan-Brazil relations would bring together complementary resources, energy capabilities and technological ambitions while giving both countries greater room to pursue their economic interests independently.

The EU has been mulling introducing the ban for months but has faced questions over how it could be enforced.
